domain: Creative Reasoning and Language and Literature

cards.q: PEN is to WRITE as KNIFE is to ___.
cards.why: A pen is the tool used for writing; a knife is the tool used for cutting. The relation is tool to function.
cards.trap: Choosing sharp or metal, which describe the knife as an object, not what it does.

cards.q: PETAL is to FLOWER as BRANCH is to ___.
cards.why: A petal is a part of a flower; a branch is a part of a tree. The relation is part to whole.
cards.trap: Choosing leaf, which is also a plant part at the same level, not the whole.

cards.q: SPARK is to FIRE as GERM is to ___.
cards.why: A spark starts a fire; a germ starts a disease. The relation is cause to effect.
cards.trap: Choosing sick, which is an adjective for a state, not the effect noun.

cards.q: WARM is to HOT as COOL is to ___.
cards.why: Warm and hot are light and strong degrees on one scale. Cool and cold mirror that same jump in degree.
cards.trap: Choosing chilly, which is only slightly stronger than cool and breaks the matched gap.

cards.q: ROSE is to FLOWER as TIGER is to ___.
cards.why: A rose is a kind of flower; a tiger is a kind of animal. The relation is member to category.
cards.trap: Choosing stripes or claw, which are parts of a tiger, not the class it belongs to.

cards.q: DOCTOR is to PATIENT as TEACHER is to ___.
cards.why: A doctor serves a patient; a teacher serves a student. The relation is professional to the person served.
cards.trap: Choosing school or lesson, which are the workplace and the material, not the person served.

cards.q: SCALPEL is to SURGEON as HAMMER is to ___.
cards.why: A scalpel is the tool a surgeon wields; a hammer is the tool a carpenter wields. Tool to user.
cards.trap: Choosing nail, which is what the hammer strikes, not who wields it.

cards.q: CHAPTER is to BOOK as SCENE is to ___.
cards.why: A chapter is a division of a book; a scene is a division of a play. Part to whole.
cards.trap: Choosing stage, which is where a play is performed, not the work that is divided.

cards.q: DRIZZLE is to DOWNPOUR as WHISPER is to ___.
cards.why: Drizzle and downpour are light and heavy rain; whisper and shout are soft and loud speech. Degree of the same act.
cards.trap: Choosing speak, the general verb, which drops the intensity relation.

cards.q: EXERCISE is to STRENGTH as STUDY is to ___.
cards.why: Exercise builds strength; study builds knowledge. The relation is activity to the result it produces.
cards.trap: Choosing book or teacher, which are inputs to study, not the result.

cards.q: THERMOMETER is to TEMPERATURE as SCALE is to ___.
cards.why: A thermometer measures temperature; a scale measures weight. Instrument to the quantity it measures.
cards.trap: Choosing time, because scale also means a timetable, which is not a measuring instrument here.

cards.q: CAUTIOUS is to PARANOID as CONFIDENT is to ___.
cards.why: Cautious is reasonable care; paranoid is that same trait in excess. Confident is reasonable self-assurance; arrogant is that trait in excess.
cards.trap: Choosing certain, which repeats the meaning of confident instead of showing its excess.

cards.q: Which word does not belong? triangle, square, circle, pentagon
cards.why: A triangle, a square, and a pentagon are polygons with straight sides and corners. A circle has no straight sides and no corners.
cards.trap: Choosing pentagon because it has the most sides, but pentagon still has straight sides and corners, so it fits the rule.

cards.q: Which does not belong? jeepney, bus, tricycle, ferry
cards.why: A jeepney, a bus, and a tricycle travel on roads. A ferry travels on water.
cards.trap: Choosing tricycle because it is the smallest vehicle, but it still runs on the road, so it fits the rule.

cards.q: Which word does not belong? happy, joyful, elated, furious
cards.why: Happy, joyful, and elated name pleasant emotions. Furious names anger.
cards.trap: Choosing elated because it looks strongest, but elated still names a pleasant emotion, so it fits the rule.

cards.q: Which number does not belong? 2, 4, 7, 8
cards.why: 2, 4, and 8 are even. 7 is the only odd number, so only that rule isolates one item.
cards.trap: Choosing 2 because it is prime, but 7 is also prime, so that rule leaves two items.

cards.q: Which does not belong? copper, iron, gold, wood
cards.why: Copper, iron, and gold are metals. Wood is not a metal.
cards.trap: Choosing gold because it is the most valuable, but gold is still a metal, so it fits the rule.

cards.q: Which does not belong? walked, jumped, sang, danced
cards.why: Walked, jumped, and danced form the past tense by adding -ed. Sang is an irregular past form.
cards.trap: Choosing danced because it has two syllables, but danced still forms its past with -ed, so it fits the rule.

cards.q: Which word does not belong? palpable, tangible, concrete, abstract
cards.why: Palpable, tangible, and concrete describe what can be perceived or touched. Abstract describes what cannot.
cards.trap: Choosing concrete because its everyday sense is building material, not the adjective in this set.

cards.q: Which does not belong? narra, molave, acacia, bamboo
cards.why: Narra, molave, and acacia are hardwood trees. Bamboo is a grass with a hollow, jointed stem.
cards.trap: Choosing acacia because it is not native, when the rule is botanical type, not origin.

cards.q: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Which conclusion must be true?
cards.why: The chain runs roses to flowers to plants, so every rose is a plant. The wrong options reverse a premise or add a claim.
cards.trap: Choosing all plants are roses, which converts the first premise illegally.

cards.q: No reptiles are warm-blooded. A gecko is a reptile. Which conclusion follows?
choices: A gecko is cold-blooded only in winter.
cards.why: The whole class reptiles lies outside warm-blooded animals, so any member lies outside too. The gecko is a member.
cards.trap: Choosing the winter option, which adds a condition the premises never state.

cards.q: If it rains, the ground gets wet. The ground is not wet. What follows?
cards.why: This is the contrapositive: if not wet, then no rain. Denying the consequent is valid reasoning.
cards.trap: Choosing wet ground means rain, which reverses the original conditional.

cards.q: Some students are athletes. All athletes train daily. Which must be true?
cards.why: The students who are athletes all train daily, so at least those students train. Nothing is said about every student or every athlete.
cards.trap: Choosing all athletes are students, which turns a particular premise into a universal one.

cards.q: Passing the test is required for the scholarship. Rico did not pass. What follows?
choices: Rico did not get the scholarship.
Rico may still get the scholarship.
cards.answer: Rico did not get the scholarship.
cards.why: A required condition is necessary: no scholarship without passing. Failing it blocks the scholarship. Passing alone does not guarantee it.
cards.trap: Choosing passing guarantees it, which treats a necessary condition as sufficient.

cards.q: All crows are black. This bird is black. Therefore this bird is a crow. What is the flaw?
choices: It treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
It generalizes from too few cases.
cards.answer: It treats a necessary condition as sufficient.
cards.why: Blackness is necessary for crows but not enough to prove crowhood, since other birds are black too. The argument affirms the consequent.
cards.trap: Choosing denies the antecedent, which is a different error about the if-clause.

cards.q: Because the witness described every detail in exact order, her account was remarkably ___.
cards.why: The clue every detail in exact order signals accuracy. Precise means exact and detailed.
cards.trap: Choosing brief because a detailed account sounds short, which the clue never says.

cards.q: The typhoon left the village ___, with no house left standing.
cards.why: No house left standing is the clue that follows the blank. Devastated means destroyed.
cards.trap: Choosing intact from habit, ignoring the phrase after the blank.

cards.q: Her apology sounded ___, so no one believed she was truly sorry.
cards.why: The result clause no one believed she was truly sorry signals a lack of sincerity.
cards.trap: Choosing sincere because apologies are expected to be sincere, ignoring the result clause.

cards.q: Although the lecture was ___, the audience stayed because the ideas were fresh.
cards.why: Although marks contrast. They stayed only because the ideas were fresh, so the lecture itself was dull.
cards.trap: Choosing lively, which agrees with fresh and removes the contrast.

cards.q: The scientist refused to publish until the results were ___, checking each trial three times.
cards.why: Checking each trial three times is the clue. Verified means confirmed as true.
cards.trap: Choosing estimated because research involves estimates, which is the opposite of triple-checking.

cards.q: The river, once ___, is now so polluted that fish cannot survive.
cards.why: Once followed by now so polluted sets a before-and-after contrast. Pristine means clean and untouched.
cards.trap: Choosing shallow because it sounds neutral, which does not contrast with polluted.

cards.q: The council's decision was ___: it satisfied neither the residents nor the developers.
cards.why: The colon explains the blank. Satisfying neither side means the decision failed both groups.
cards.trap: Choosing final because decisions are often final, which the explanation does not support.

cards.q: Despite the committee's ___ reputation, its latest findings were met with open skepticism.
cards.why: Despite signals contrast. Skepticism came anyway, so the reputation had to be excellent. Sterling means of the highest quality.
cards.trap: Choosing dubious, which agrees with skepticism and cancels the contrast.

cards.q: The judge found the testimony credible. Credible means ___.
cards.why: Credible comes from the Latin credere, to believe. A credible testimony can be believed.
cards.trap: Choosing hearsay because both are courtroom words, but hearsay names a kind of evidence.

cards.q: The plan was feasible given the budget. Feasible means ___.
cards.why: Feasible means capable of being done. The phrase given the budget shows the plan can be carried out within it.
cards.trap: Choosing already approved because feasible sounds official, but approval is a separate step.

cards.q: The manager's abrupt reply surprised the staff. Abrupt means ___.
cards.why: Abrupt describes something that starts or ends without warning and often lacks courtesy. The staff's surprise supports that sense.
cards.trap: Choosing carefully planned, which contradicts the surprise the reply caused.

cards.q: Her remarks were ambiguous. Ambiguous means ___.
choices: open to more than one meaning
cards.answer: open to more than one meaning
cards.why: Ambiguous means admitting more than one interpretation. The prefix ambi- means both.
cards.trap: Choosing clearly false because ambiguity feels like a flaw, but it is unclearness, not falsity.

cards.q: Later studies corroborate the first findings. Corroborate means ___.
cards.why: To corroborate is to strengthen a claim by adding independent evidence. Later studies doing this confirm the first findings.
cards.trap: Choosing replace completely because newer studies often supersede old ones, which is not corroboration.

cards.q: The senator's speech was a diatribe against the bill. Diatribe means ___.
cards.why: A diatribe is a forceful and bitter verbal attack. The words against the bill signal opposition, not summary.
cards.trap: Choosing careful summary because speeches often summarize, but diatribe names hostility.

cards.q: Each of the contestants ___ a number before the round begins.
cards.why: Each is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes a singular verb. The plural noun after of does not control the verb.
cards.trap: Choosing have because contestants, the nearest noun, is plural.

cards.q: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ ready when the bell rang.
cards.why: With neither nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Students is plural, so the verb is were.
cards.trap: Choosing was because neither looks singular at the start of the sentence.

cards.q: The committee acted as a single body and released ___ decision.
cards.why: Committee is a collective noun acting as one unit, so it takes the singular possessive its.
cards.trap: Choosing their because a committee is made of many people.

cards.q: Between you and ___, the plan needs another review.
cards.why: Between is a preposition, so it takes the object form. Me is the object pronoun and I is the subject form.
cards.trap: Choosing I because it sounds more formal after and.

cards.q: By the time the bell rang, the students ___ the experiment.
cards.why: The finishing happened before another past event, so the past perfect had finished is required.
cards.trap: Choosing have finished, which ties the action to the present instead of an earlier past.

cards.q: Choose the sentence with consistent tense.
choices: She opened the folder and read the letter.
She opened the folder and reads the letter.
She opens the folder and read the letter.
She had opened the folder and reads the letter.
cards.answer: She opened the folder and read the letter.
cards.why: Two actions joined by and in one past time frame must both be past. Opened and read are both past forms.
cards.trap: Choosing a version that pairs a past verb with a present verb mid-sentence.

cards.q: Which revision fixes the dangling modifier in: Walking home, the rain soaked me.
choices: Walking home, I was soaked by the rain.
Walking home, the rain soaked my bag.
The rain soaked me, walking home.
cards.answer: Walking home, I was soaked by the rain.
cards.why: The opening phrase must describe the subject. In the original the rain seems to walk. In the answer I does the walking.
cards.trap: Choosing the version that changes the object, not the misplaced subject.

cards.q: The job requires typing reports, answering calls, and ___.
cards.why: Items in a series must be parallel. Typing and answering are gerunds, so the third item must also be a gerund.
cards.trap: Choosing to file records because it sounds right after requires, but it breaks the series pattern.

cards.q: The applicant is honest, hardworking, and ___.
cards.why: The series lists adjectives, so the third item must be one adjective. Punctual matches honest and hardworking.
cards.trap: Choosing always on time because the meaning fits, but it is a phrase, not an adjective.

cards.q: There ___ several reasons for the delay in the project.
cards.why: In a there sentence the verb agrees with the noun that follows it. Reasons is plural, so the verb is are.
cards.trap: Choosing is because there appears to be the subject.

cards.q: The new policy is more effective than ___.
cards.why: A comparison must compare like with like. A policy must be compared with another policy, so the old one is correct.
cards.trap: Choosing any policy, which includes the new policy itself, so the comparison is illogical.

cards.q: The book ___ cover is torn belongs to the library.
cards.why: Whose shows possession. The cover belongs to the book, so whose is the correct relative pronoun.
cards.trap: Choosing which because the antecedent is a thing, but which cannot show possession.

cards.q: Which sentence uses the comma correctly?
choices: Although it rained, the game resumed.
Although, it rained the game resumed.
Although it rained the game, resumed.
Although it rained; the game resumed.
cards.answer: Although it rained, the game resumed.
cards.why: An introductory dependent clause takes a comma before the main clause. The other options place the mark between the wrong words.
cards.trap: Choosing the semicolon version, which needs independent clauses on both sides.

cards.q: Which mark correctly joins two independent clauses that share no conjunction?
cards.why: A semicolon links two independent clauses without a conjunction. A comma alone would create a run-on.
cards.trap: Choosing the colon, which introduces an explanation or a list rather than linking equal clauses.

cards.q: Choose the correct possessive form: the reports of the two students.
cards.why: Two students is a plural noun ending in s, so the possessive adds only an apostrophe after that s.
cards.trap: Choosing the student's reports, which is singular and names only one student.

cards.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: The results were clear; however, the method was flawed.
The results were clear, however, the method was flawed.
The results were clear however; the method was flawed.
The results were clear: however the method was flawed.
cards.answer: The results were clear; however, the method was flawed.
cards.why: However is a conjunctive adverb. Two independent clauses joined this way need a semicolon before however and a comma after it.
cards.trap: Choosing the comma-only version, which is a comma splice.

cards.q: Choose the correctly capitalized sentence.
choices: My aunt teaches Filipino at the University of the Philippines.
My Aunt teaches Filipino at the University of the Philippines.
My aunt teaches filipino at the University of the Philippines.
My aunt teaches Filipino at the university of the Philippines.
cards.answer: My aunt teaches Filipino at the University of the Philippines.
cards.why: Filipino names a language and takes a capital. The full name University of the Philippines is also capitalized. Aunt stays lowercase after a possessive.
cards.trap: Choosing the version with Aunt capitalized, which is wrong because the word follows a possessive, not a title.

cards.q: The kit contained three items ___ a ruler, a compass, and a protractor.
cards.why: A colon introduces a list after a complete clause. The words the kit contained three items can stand alone.
cards.trap: Choosing the comma, which fuses the independent clause with the list.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: Her voice was like velvet. Which figure of speech is used?
cards.why: Like signals an explicit comparison between two unlike things, which is a simile.
cards.trap: Choosing metaphor, which compares without like or as.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: Time is a thief. Which figure of speech is used?
cards.why: Time is called a thief directly, with no like or as. An implied comparison of this kind is a metaphor.
cards.trap: Choosing simile because a comparison is present, but simile needs an explicit like or as.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: The wind whispered through the trees. Which figure of speech is used?
cards.why: Whispering is a human act given to the wind, which is personification.
cards.trap: Choosing metaphor because whisper is figurative, but the specific pattern gives a human act to a nonhuman thing.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: I have told you a million times. Which figure of speech is used?
cards.why: A million times is deliberate exaggeration for emphasis, not a literal count.
cards.trap: Choosing irony because the sentence sounds accusing, but irony reverses meaning instead of exaggerating.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: A fire station burns to the ground. Which literary device best describes this?
cards.why: The outcome reverses expectation: the building meant to stop fires is destroyed by one. That gap is situational irony.
cards.trap: Choosing oxymoron because fire station sounds contradictory, but an oxymoron is a phrase pairing opposites.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: He met his Waterloo in the final round. Which literary device is used?
cards.why: Waterloo refers to the defeat of Napoleon, a well-known event. An indirect reference of this kind is an allusion.
cards.trap: Choosing hyperbole because the defeat sounds overstated, but no exaggeration is present.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: The room fell into a deafening silence. Which figure of speech is used?
cards.why: Deafening and silence are contradictory terms joined in one phrase, which is an oxymoron.
cards.trap: Choosing hyperbole because deafening is extreme, but the device turns on contradiction, not exaggeration.

cards.sub: Figures of Speech and Literary Devices
cards.q: All hands on deck. Which figure of speech is used?
cards.why: Hands stands for the whole sailors. Naming a part to mean the whole is synecdoche.
cards.trap: Choosing metaphor because hands is not literal, but the figure is a part-for-whole substitution.

cards.q: Read the passage. The Philippine eagle nests only in old-growth forest, and a pair raises one chick every two years. Logging removes the tall trees the bird needs. Conservation groups now pay forest guards to protect known nesting sites. The eagle's survival depends less on breeding programs than on keeping the forest standing. What is the main idea?
choices: Protecting old-growth forest matters more to the eagle than breeding programs.
Breeding programs have already saved the Philippine eagle.
Logging companies pay the forest guards.
The eagle raises many chicks each year.
cards.answer: Protecting old-growth forest matters more to the eagle than breeding programs.
cards.why: The passage ends by weighing breeding programs against keeping the forest standing and favors the forest.
cards.trap: Choosing the breeding option because breeding is mentioned, though the passage says survival depends less on it.

cards.q: Read the passage. The Philippine eagle pairs for life and raises one chick every two years. A chick stays with its parents for about a year and a half. How often does a pair raise a chick?
cards.why: The passage states one chick every two years directly.
cards.trap: Choosing every year because the chick stays a year and a half, which is a different fact.

cards.q: Read the passage. The mangrove cutters were told to stop. Within a year the shallow water cleared and small fish returned. By the third year, fishers who had left the village were setting nets again. No one had restocked the fish. What can be inferred about the fish?
choices: The mangrove forest had sheltered them.
They were brought in from another village.
They were restocked by the government.
They returned because the water warmed.
cards.answer: The mangrove forest had sheltered them.
cards.why: The fish returned once cutting stopped, and no one restocked them, so the mangrove itself supported them.
cards.trap: Choosing the restocking option even though the last sentence denies it.

cards.q: Read the passage. The Spanish arrived in 1565. Long before that, oral epics were chanted in many communities. Missionaries later wrote some down but edited out passages they judged immoral. Today scholars compare those records with versions still sung in upland villages. The comparison shows what the friars changed, and what they missed. What is the main idea?
choices: Comparing old records with living songs reveals what missionaries altered.
Oral epics were never written down.
Missionaries preserved epics without any changes.
Upland villages no longer sing epics.
cards.answer: Comparing old records with living songs reveals what missionaries altered.
cards.why: The passage centers on the comparison and on what it reveals about the friars' edits and omissions.
cards.trap: Choosing the preservation option, which contradicts edited out passages they judged immoral.

cards.q: Read the passage. During the Spanish period, possession of Rizal's novels could draw suspicion. Copies entered the islands in luggage and crates, and readers lent worn copies to trusted friends. Officials seized what they found, but the books kept circulating. What does the passage suggest about the seizures?
choices: They did not stop the books from circulating.
They raised the price of the novels.
cards.answer: They did not stop the books from circulating.
cards.why: Seizures happened, yet smuggling and private lending kept the novels moving, so the seizures failed to end circulation.
cards.trap: Choosing that they never happened, which the text denies by stating officials seized what they found.

cards.q: Read the passage. The jeepney began with surplus military jeeps left in the islands after 1945. Owners lengthened the chassis and added benches to carry more riders. By the 1970s, local shops were building units from scratch, and the vehicle later became a national icon. Where did the first jeepneys come from?
choices: Local shops building units from scratch
Imported buses from the United States
cards.why: The first sentence names surplus military jeeps left after 1945 as the origin.
cards.trap: Choosing local shops because the passage mentions them, but that happened later, by the 1970s.

cards.q: Read the passage. Rice terraces in the Cordillera were built by hand over centuries. Each wall holds soil against erosion on steep slopes. Water comes from communal forests above the fields, so those forests are part of the irrigation system. When the forests are cut, the terraces fail. What is the author's main purpose?
choices: To explain why the terraces depend on the forest above them
To describe how rice is cooked in the Cordillera
To argue that the terraces should be abandoned
To list the tools used to build the terraces
cards.answer: To explain why the terraces depend on the forest above them
cards.why: The passage traces water from forest to terrace and closes with the consequence of cutting the forest.
cards.trap: Choosing the abandon option because the last sentence warns of failure, but no recommendation is made.

cards.q: Read the passage. The barangay captain promised shade for every street. Two years later the saplings stand in neat rows, each staked, watered, and wrapped in a plastic sleeve. It is a fine plan. The trees, however, are still in the nursery. What is the tone of the last two sentences?
cards.why: It is a fine plan praises the scheme, then however undercuts it: no trees were planted. The effect is dry skepticism.
cards.trap: Choosing strictly neutral because the facts are plain, but the however reversal carries judgment.

cards.q: Who wrote Noli Me Tangere?
cards.why: Rizal published Noli Me Tangere in 1887, a novel that exposed abuses under Spanish rule.
cards.trap: Choosing Balagtas because both wrote in the Spanish period, but he wrote Florante at Laura.

cards.q: Who wrote Florante at Laura?
cards.why: Balagtas wrote the awit Florante at Laura, published in 1838 and set in Albania.
cards.trap: Choosing Rizal because both authors wrote under Spanish rule.

cards.q: Who wrote the short story Footnote to Youth?
cards.why: Villa wrote Footnote to Youth, a story about a young man who marries early and later sees his son repeat the choice.
cards.trap: Choosing Joaquin because both are major English-language writers of the same period.

cards.q: Who wrote May Day Eve?
cards.why: May Day Eve is a Joaquin story about memory, a mirror, and a prophecy that shapes a marriage.
cards.trap: Choosing Arcellana because both wrote in English during the same postwar period.

cards.q: Who wrote Dekada '70?
cards.why: Bautista wrote Dekada '70, a novel about one family's life under martial law.
cards.trap: Choosing Hernandez because he also wrote social fiction, but his novels are in Filipino and earlier.

cards.q: Which is the earliest known book printed in the Philippines?
cards.why: The Doctrina Christiana was printed in Manila in 1593, which makes it the earliest known book printed in the country.
cards.trap: Choosing Urbana at Felisa because it is also an old didactic text, but it appeared in 1864.
